title: Shannon Source Coding Theorem — Module Overview
content:
This module formalizes Shannon's source coding theorem (1948): the entropy $H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)$ is the fundamental limit of lossless data compression. Data from a source with entropy $H$ can be compressed to $H + \varepsilon$ bits per symbol (for any $\varepsilon > 0$), but not below $H$ bits per symbol, with asymptotically zero error probability. This is the 'data compression' half of Shannon's foundational 1948 paper, complementing the channel coding theorem (see `shannon-channel-coding`).

The development is organized into four theorem stubs following the standard textbook proof: AEP → typical set bounds → achievability → converse. The `import Mathlib` on line 9 brings in the full Mathlib library; a genuine formalization would specifically need `MeasureTheory.Probability`, `Analysis.SpecialFunctions.Log`, and `Probability.ProbabilityMassFunction`. The `InformationTheory.SourceCoding` namespace scopes all four theorems.
mathContext: Shannon source coding: for an i.i.d. source $X_1, X_2, \ldots \sim p$ with entropy $H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x)\log_2 p(x)$, lossless compression to rate $R$ bits/symbol is achievable with vanishing error iff $R > H(X)$. The entropy ranges from 0 (deterministic source) to $\log_2|\mathcal{X}|$ (uniform source).

title: Asymptotic Equipartition Property (AEP)
content:
The AEP states that for i.i.d. sequences, the normalized log-probability converges to the entropy: $-\frac{1}{n}\log p(X_1,\ldots,X_n) \to H(X)$ in probability. This is the information-theoretic analogue of the law of large numbers — in fact, it IS the weak law applied to the random variables $Y_i = -\log p(X_i)$, which are i.i.d. with $E[Y_i] = H(X)$.

The AEP partitions sequences into a 'typical set' of roughly $2^{nH}$ sequences that carry almost all the probability, and an 'atypical set' of negligible probability. This concentration phenomenon is why compression works: we need only encode the typical sequences.

The type signature `{p : α → ℝ} (hp : ∀ x, 0 < p x) (hsum : ∑ x, p x = 1)` represents a strictly positive probability distribution on a finite alphabet. The strict positivity `0 < p x` (rather than `0 ≤ p x`) ensures $\log p(x)$ is well-defined for all $x$. Currently a placeholder proving `True`.
mathContext:
$-\frac{1}{n}\log p(X_1^n) = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log p(X_i) \xrightarrow{P} E[-\log p(X)] = H(X)$ as $n \to \infty$.

This is the WLLN for $Y_i = -\log p(X_i)$: $\bar{Y}_n \xrightarrow{P} E[Y] = H(X)$.

Strengthening: McMillan (1953) proved $-\frac{1}{n}\log p(X_1^n) \to H(X)$ a.s. (strong AEP) for ergodic sources, extending beyond i.i.d.

title: Typical Set Size Bound
content:
The typical set $A_\varepsilon^{(n)}$ contains sequences whose empirical entropy is within $\varepsilon$ of $H(X)$. Three key properties:

(1) **Upper bound**: $|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \leq 2^{n(H+\varepsilon)}$ — proved by noting each typical sequence has probability $\geq 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}$, and total probability $\leq 1$.

(2) **Lower bound**: $|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \geq (1-\varepsilon)2^{n(H-\varepsilon)}$ for large $n$ — since $\Pr[A_\varepsilon^{(n)}] \geq 1-\varepsilon$ and each element has probability $\leq 2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}$.

(3) **High probability**: $\Pr[A_\varepsilon^{(n)}] \to 1$ by the AEP.

Together these pin down the typical set size as $\approx 2^{nH}$, which is exponentially smaller than $|\mathcal{X}|^n$ when $H < \log|\mathcal{X}|$ (i.e., whenever the source is not uniform). The theorem has additional parameters `{n : ℕ} {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) (hn : 0 < n)` ensuring positive block length and tolerance.
mathContext:
$A_\varepsilon^{(n)} = \{x^n \in \mathcal{X}^n : |{-\frac{1}{n}\log p(x^n)} - H(X)| \leq \varepsilon\}$.

Upper bound proof: $1 \geq \sum_{x^n \in A_\varepsilon^{(n)}} p(x^n) \geq |A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \cdot 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}$, so $|A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \leq 2^{n(H+\varepsilon)}$.

Example: binary source with $p(0)=0.9$, $H \approx 0.469$ bits. For $n=100$: typical set has $\approx 2^{47}$ sequences out of $2^{100}$ total — a fraction $\approx 2^{-53}$.

title: Source Coding Achievability
content:
Achievability: assign unique $\lceil n(H+\varepsilon) \rceil$-bit codewords to each typical sequence (there are at most $2^{n(H+\varepsilon)}$ of them). Atypical sequences are flagged with a special prefix bit and encoded with $n\log|\mathcal{X}|$ bits. Since $\Pr[\text{atypical}] \to 0$ by the AEP, the error probability vanishes and the rate $H + \varepsilon + O(1/n)$ is achievable for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

This is the fundamental reason entropy measures compressibility: the number of 'likely' sequences grows as $2^{nH}$, so $H$ bits per symbol suffice to distinguish them. The proof is constructive — it describes an explicit coding scheme — though impractical for large $n$ (the codebook has $2^{nH}$ entries). Practical algorithms (Huffman, arithmetic coding, Lempel-Ziv) achieve the same limit via different mechanisms.

The Lean statement takes `{ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε)` as parameters, encoding the 'for any $\varepsilon > 0$' quantifier in the theorem statement.
mathContext:
For rate $R = H(X) + \varepsilon$ ($\varepsilon > 0$):

Code construction: enumerate typical sequences as $1, 2, \ldots, |A_\varepsilon^{(n)}|$ using $\lceil \log_2 |A_\varepsilon^{(n)}| \rceil \leq n(H+\varepsilon) + 1$ bits. Prefix with 0 for typical, 1 for atypical.

Rate: $\frac{n(H+\varepsilon) + 2}{n} = H + \varepsilon + \frac{2}{n} \to H + \varepsilon$.

Error probability: $P_e^{(n)} = \Pr[X^n \notin A_\varepsilon^{(n)}] \to 0$ by AEP.

title: Shared Type Signature: Finite Alphabet with Positive Distribution
content:
All four theorems share the parameter pattern `{α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {p : α → ℝ} (hp : ∀ x, 0 < p x) (hsum : ∑ x, p x = 1)`. This encodes a discrete probability distribution on a finite alphabet:

- `Fintype α`: the alphabet is finite (needed for finite sums)
- `DecidableEq α`: equality on alphabet elements is decidable (needed for counting)
- `p : α → ℝ`: probability mass function as a real-valued function
- `hp : ∀ x, 0 < p x`: strict positivity prevents $\log 0$ and ensures full support
- `hsum : ∑ x, p x = 1`: normalization to a valid probability distribution

A more idiomatic Lean formalization might use Mathlib's `PMF α` (probability mass function) or `MeasureTheory.IsProbabilityMeasure` instead of raw functions with manual constraints. The strict positivity constraint is mathematically natural here: zero-probability symbols can be removed from the alphabet without loss of generality.
mathContext: The constraints encode: $p \in \Delta_{|\mathcal{X}|}^\circ = \{p \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{X}|} : p_i > 0,\, \sum_i p_i = 1\}$ — the interior of the probability simplex. Strict positivity is needed because $H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$ uses $\log p(x)$, and $\lim_{p \to 0^+} p\log p = 0$ makes the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$ standard but requires careful handling in formal proofs.

title: Placeholder Pattern: True as Proof Stub
content:
Each theorem body is `True := trivial` — a placeholder stub that type-checks but proves nothing. This is a common pattern in Lean for work-in-progress formalizations: the theorem statements (types) encode the mathematical claims, while the proofs (terms) are deferred.

The correct conclusion type for `aep_convergence` would involve measure-theoretic probability: something like `∀ ε > 0, Filter.Tendsto (fun n => Pr[|(-1/n) * ∑ i in range n, log (p (X i)) - H| > ε]) atTop (nhds 0)` — requiring product measures, i.i.d. random variables, and the WLLN from Mathlib. The gap between `True` and this correct type reflects the current state of probability formalization in Lean 4: Mathlib has measure theory infrastructure but formalizing i.i.d. sequences and their properties remains challenging.
mathContext:
The correct statement would be: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \Pr\left[\left|-\frac{1}{n}\log p(X_1^n) - H(X)\right| > \varepsilon\right] \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

This requires: (1) product probability space $(\mathcal{X}^n, p^{\otimes n})$; (2) the random variable $-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log p(X_i)$; (3) the WLLN: $\bar{Y}_n \xrightarrow{P} \mu$ when $Y_i$ are i.i.d. with $E[Y_i] = \mu$.
